Define a timeline. List three things a timeline helps a historian see.
questions.answer: A timeline is a line on which events are placed in the order they happened, with spacing reflecting elapsed time. It helps a historian see (i) the ORDER of events, (ii) the DURATION of an event or reign, and (iii) SIMULTANEITY — what was happening at the same time in different places.

questions.question: How many years passed between 1500 BCE and 500 CE? Show working.
questions.answer: From 1500 BCE to 1 BCE = 1499 years. Then 1 BCE to 1 CE = 1 year (no year zero). Then 1 CE to 500 CE = 499 years. Total = 1499 + 1 + 499 = 1999 years. Shortcut: 1500 + 500 − 1 = 1999.
questions.explanation: Add and subtract 1 for the missing year zero.

questions.question: Name the three families of historical sources and give one example of each.
questions.answer: (i) Archaeological — pottery / coins / ruins. (ii) Literary — Vedas / Tripiṭakas / inscriptions. (iii) Oral — folk songs / family genealogies passed down across generations.

questions.question: Explain stratigraphy in your own words and why it is useful to archaeologists.
questions.answer: Stratigraphy is the study of the LAYERS (strata) of soil at an archaeological site. Older layers lie deeper; newer layers lie above. So if two objects are found at the same site, the deeper one is older. This gives archaeologists a relative order of objects without any chemistry — just by where they were buried.

questions.question: Why are Ashoka's edicts especially valuable to historians?
questions.answer: They were carved in stone in the 3rd century BCE — at the time of the events — across the subcontinent, so they are widespread and survive well. They tell us about Ashoka's policies, his concern for his subjects, and his use of moral law (dhamma). They are direct evidence rather than a later retelling.

questions.question: A king's inscription claims he won every battle he fought. How would you, as a historian, decide whether to believe it?
questions.answer: I would ask WHO made it (the king himself or his official) — he has reason to praise himself. I would ask WHAT it leaves out — defeats, taxes, hardships. I would look for OTHER sources: a rival king's inscription, a foreign traveller's account, archaeological evidence (destroyed forts, treaties, coin distribution). Only if independent sources agree would I treat the claim as reliable.

questions.question: Compare archaeological, literary and oral sources. For each, give one strength and one limitation, with an example.
questions.answer: Archaeological (e.g. pottery, coins, ruins): STRENGTH — physical evidence that survives long, not biased by who 'wrote' it. LIMITATION — silent on names and ideas; we rarely know WHO used the object. Literary (e.g. Vedas, inscriptions, Sangam poetry): STRENGTH — gives names, dates, ideas, laws, moral views. LIMITATION — usually written by a small literate elite, can be biased toward kings or priests. Oral (e.g. folk songs, family genealogies): STRENGTH — preserves community memory across centuries, including ordinary people. LIMITATION — small details shift over time; harder to date precisely. The best history uses all three together.
questions.explanation: Strengths and weaknesses of each source family.

questions.question: An archaeologist excavates a site and finds, from top to bottom: (i) iron tools, (ii) bronze tools, (iii) painted pottery, (iv) charcoal. (a) Order the layers from oldest to most recent. (b) Which item could be radiocarbon-dated, and why? (c) What does this tell you about the people who lived here?
questions.answer: (a) Older lies deeper. So oldest → most recent: charcoal (deepest) → painted pottery → bronze tools → iron tools (top). (b) Charcoal can be radiocarbon-dated because it is once-living organic material; C-14 can date it. The painted pottery and metal tools cannot be C-14 dated unless they have organic remains stuck to them. (c) The site shows a long sequence of habitation: an early people who used fire (charcoal), then a culture making painted pottery, then bronze users, and finally iron users. This is the typical Stone → Bronze → Iron progression seen at many ancient sites.
questions.explanation: Stratigraphy gives order; C-14 needs organics; cultural sequence.
